content_units: Velvet & Vice: Dinner Party Concept
A witty, low-improv murder mystery for   8 adults   on   Saturday, 2026-11-14, 19:00-22:00  .
Theme: a glamorous 1930s-style private supper at an upscale hotel club where charm, gossip, and a missing fortune turn deadly.
Core vibe
- Clever and stylish, not scary
- Script-supported so shy guests are comfortable
- Strong secrets and motives, but light social pressure
- Designed to unfold cleanly over dinner in 3 hours
The Gilded Fox Supper Club: Roles, Clues, and Party Flow
Party setting

Welcome guests to   The Gilded Fox Supper Club  , an exclusive late-night dining room inside a fashionable city hotel in 1934. The owner is unveiling a new investment scheme and a rumored engagement. Before dessert, the host is found dead after a toast, and everyone at the table has a reason to lie.
Why this works for your group
- Witty banter fits better than horror
- Characters can be played broadly or quietly
- Guests get structured prompts instead of needing constant improvisation
- The mystery can be solved through clue cards, not acting skill
Character lineup
Give each guest an envelope with:
- character summary
- public persona
- private secret
- 2 conversation goals
- 1 item/clue to reveal only when prompted
Option 1:   Vivian Vale, nightclub singer     Glamorous star with debts and a sharp tongue   Knows who was being blackmailed
Role Card
Option 2:   Cedric March, hotel owner     Smooth investor hosting the supper   Planned to cut someone out of a deal
Role Card
Option 3:   Beatrice Thorne, society columnist     Collects scandals for tomorrow's paper   Has a damaging photo hidden in her bag
Role Card
Option 4:   Arthur Finch, solicitor     Precise, dry, and always listening   Altered a legal document earlier that day
Role Card
Option 5:   Nora Bell, head chef     Fiercely proud of the supper club   Overheard a kitchen-side argument
Role Card
Option 6:   Julian Frost, charming magician     Entertainer hired for the evening   Can account for missing objects but not his motives
Role Card
Option 7:   Eleanor Price, art dealer     Elegant guest chasing investors   Sold a fake piece to someone at the table
Role Card
Option 8:   Thomas Reed, radio presenter     Cheerful public voice with private debts   Heard a key conversation through a live mic test
Role Card
Best roles for your two shy guests
Assign the shy guests roles with clear structure and lower performance pressure:
-   Arthur Finch  : observant, dry humor, can contribute by “noting inconsistencies”
-   Nora Bell  : practical witness role with strong factual clues
- Alternate low-improv options:   Thomas Reed   or   Eleanor Price
For those envelopes, add:
- 3 ready-made lines they can read if stuck
- 2 direct questions to ask others
- 1 timed reveal card saying exactly when to speak
Mystery structure
Victim:   Cedric March, the hotel owner
Cause of death:   poison slipped into his post-toast digestif

True solution:   Beatrice Thorne poisoned Cedric after learning he intended to expose her fabricated gossip racket and sue her for blackmail. She framed Nora by planting a kitchen vial and relied on everyone else’s scandals to muddy the room.
Everyone still has a motive  , which keeps the mystery lively:
- Vivian needed money and feared public disgrace
- Arthur altered paperwork for Cedric
- Nora was being blamed for missing supplies
- Julian was paid to distract guests during a private exchange
- Eleanor faced exposure over forged artwork
- Thomas owed money and hoped for sponsorship
- Beatrice faced ruin if Cedric spoke first
Clue release plan
Use   3 rounds   of clue cards so the night stays organized.
Round   Time   What guests learn   Host action
1. Aperitif Secrets   19:20   Motives, rivalries, missing contract, overheard argument   Hand each guest 1 private clue card
2. The Body & The Room   20:05   Cedric collapses; glass residue, altered seating, broken compact mirror   Read incident card; place 3 shared clues on table
3. Final Revelations   21:00   Fake alibi exposed, planted vial discovered, newspaper draft found   Deliver final envelopes; begin accusations
Specific clue kit
Prepare these simple physical clues:
- a torn contract page
- a fake society column draft
- a labeled “kitchen tonic” vial
- a lipstick-marked napkin
- a seating card with one name crossed out
- a burned note reading “midnight ledger”
- a pocket watch stopped at 20:03
- a photo print or handwritten note linking Beatrice to blackmail
Best structure:
- 1 private clue per guest at arrival
- 3 shared clues at the “murder” moment
- 1 final reveal per guest before accusations
That gives enough evidence without overwhelming people.
19:00-22:00 Hosting Timeline
19:00-19:20 — Arrival and warm-up
- Offer a welcome drink
- Give name cards and character envelopes
- Ask everyone to mingle in character lightly
- Use a simple opener: “What brings you to the Gilded Fox tonight?”
19:20-19:50 — First course and social secrets
- Guests share their public backstory
- Host circulates and nudges conversation with prompt cards
- Quietly distribute Round 1 clues
- Keep tone playful, with gossip and witty suspicion
19:50-20:05 — The toast and the murder
- Announce Cedric’s toast and upcoming “business reveal”
- Read a short scripted toast
- Cedric drinks, staggers, and is declared dead
- Pause 2 minutes for dramatic reaction, then continue dinner
20:05-20:45 — Investigation over main course
- Place shared evidence on the table
- Guests question one another using prompt cards
- Encourage each person to reveal one secret
- Keep the shy guests involved by directly asking factual questions
20:45-21:00 — Intermission and private theories
- Clear plates, refresh drinks
- Hand out Round 3 clues
- Ask guests to write their top suspect and reason
21:00-21:35 — Accusations and final statements
- Go around the table for 30-second accusations
- Allow each suspect a short defense
- Take a final vote
- Reveal the murderer and explain the clue chain
21:35-22:00 — Awards and unwind
- Give funny awards: Best Alibi, Sharpest Detective, Most Dramatic Reveal
- Drop character voice and serve dessert/coffee
- Let guests compare what they missed
Costumes, Menu Style, and Easy Host Setup
Simple costume ideas
Keep it easy and affordable:
-   All guests  : black, gold, cream, or jewel tones
-   Men or masc-presenting  : shirt, vest, blazer, suspenders, pocket square
-   Women or femme-presenting  : satin blouse, beaded jewelry, gloves, hair clip, long skirt or black dress
-   Universal accessories  : fake pearls, scarf, hat, brooch, notebook, gloves
Character-specific easy add-ons:
- Vivian: long gloves or dramatic earrings
- Arthur: spectacles, notebook, tie
- Nora: apron at arrival, then remove for dinner
- Julian: deck of cards
- Beatrice: feathered headband or press notebook
- Thomas: vintage-style microphone prop or cue cards
Menu style that fits the mystery
Choose food that is easy to serve without disrupting the game:
- starter: tomato soup shooters or small tartlets
- main: baked pasta, roast chicken, or mushroom pie with salad
- dessert: chocolate mousse, tiramisu cups, or mini tarts
Best hosting choice:
-   Serve plated starter, buffet-style main, plated dessert
- This keeps you out of the kitchen during the clue-heavy middle section
Room setup
- one main table with name cards
- side table for clue props
- jazz playlist at low volume
- warm lamps or candles
- printed menu using the venue name:   The Gilded Fox Supper Club
Host script tips
Use short scripted moments so the night never stalls:
- opening welcome: 45 seconds
- toast before murder: 30 seconds
- investigation reset: “Everyone now shares one thing they have not yet admitted.”
- accusation round: 1 sentence per person
- solution reveal: 2-3 minutes maximum
Quick Actions
Invite Text
Character Sheets
Jazz Playlist
Editable Menus
Ready-to-use host notes
Opening line
“Welcome to The Gilded Fox Supper Club, where the wine is expensive, the smiles are polished, and at least one person here should be very nervous.”
Toast line
“To profitable partnerships, discreet friendships, and a future in which all accounts are finally settled.”
How to make it easy for shy guests
- give them fact-based roles, not flamboyant ones
- include 3 prewritten lines in their envelope
- let them reveal clues by reading cards aloud
- ask table-wide questions so they are not forced into one-on-one improvisation
How to keep the tone witty
- lean into scandal, ego, and bad manners rather than menace
- reward clever accusations, not loud acting
- keep any “death” description brief and clean
- use playful awards at the end
Best final format for your night
If you want the smoothest version, run it as:
-   19:00 arrival cocktails
-   19:20 first course + secrets
-   20:00 murder reveal
-   20:05 investigation over dinner
-   21:00 final clues + accusations
-   21:35 solution + dessert
This concept is complete as-is and well matched to   8 adults  ,   3 hours  ,   witty tone  , and   low-pressure improvisation  .
